passage:
The email arrived at four: the Bengaluru firm wanted an answer by eight that evening. Jagdish sat on the stairs while rain hammered the roof and the power went out. He had never lived away from his parents, whose small tailoring shop relied on his help with the bills and the delivery scooter. His sister Jyoti climbed up with two cups of tea. "You haven't eaten. What's the real problem?"
"If I go, who does the bills? If I stay, I'll always wonder."
"Then let's write it down. I'll learn the bills from you this month. You visit every second month. And we ask Papa and Amma tonight."
By phone torch they talked with their parents until seven-forty, and Jagdish replied yes, with a start date in six weeks.

qa.q: By what time did the Bengaluru firm want an answer?
qa.a: The firm wanted an answer by eight that evening.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: He was torn between guilt about leaving the shop and the fear of always wondering, shown in his words about the bills and about staying.

qa.q: What turning point turned the dilemma into a plan?
qa.a: Jyoti asked what the real problem was and proposed learning the bills, planned visits and asking their parents that night, so the choice became a shared plan.

qa.q: What might Papa and Amma have felt when they heard the plan that evening?
qa.a: They may have felt both worry about the shop and pride in Jagdish, since they talked the plan through and Jagdish said yes only after the conversation.

grounding: A young adult offered a job in another city weighs growth against parents' needs, and honest talk and shared plans reduce the sense of betrayal.

passage:
Dolma read the offer letter for the third time on the terrace of their Delhi flat: a research post in Hyderabad, starting in April. Her younger sister Avni sat cross-legged nearby with a maths book, watching her.
"You've been quiet since morning."
"Papa and Mama are used to me being around on Sundays. If I go, it feels like leaving them."
"Or like doing your work," said Avni. "Did you ask them?"
At dinner Dolma put the letter on the table. Her father read it slowly. "We will miss you at Sunday lunch. But we would miss more if you stayed and grew sour." Her mother laughed. "Video call every Sunday, and you come in Losar." Dolma exhaled for the first time in days.

qa.q: Where is the research post that Dolma was offered?
qa.a: The research post is in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling as she read the offer letter on the terrace?
qa.a: She felt torn and guilty, worried that going would feel like leaving her parents even though the post was work she wanted.

qa.q: What choice moved Dolma from worrying alone to a shared plan?
qa.a: She took Avni's advice to ask her parents and put the letter on the table at dinner, and they agreed on Sunday video calls and a visit at Losar.

qa.q: How does Dolma's father see her leaving?
qa.a: He says the family will miss her at Sunday lunch but would miss more if she stayed and grew sour, so he treats her growth as important too.

grounding: A young adult offered a job in another city weighs personal growth against parents' needs, and honest talk and shared plans reduce betrayal.

passage:
"Tarun, I got the Bengaluru offer."
"That's amazing! Why do you look like that?"
"Because of Papa. Since Amma passed, he's alone. If I go, who'll take him to his check-ups? Who'll eat dinner with him?"
"Thomas, he's not helpless."
"He's lonely. I see it."
"And if you stay, you'll resent it. You've wanted this job for three years."
"So what do I do? Either way I'm selfish."
"Neither way is selfish. Talk to him. Properly."
That evening, Thomas sat with his father. "Papa, I got an offer in Bengaluru. I want it. But I'm worried about you."
His father smiled slowly. "I'm worried about me too. But I'd be more worried if you stayed for me."
They made a plan: Tarun would take Papa to check-ups; Thomas would call every night and come home one weekend a month.

qa.q: How long has Thomas wanted this job?
qa.a: Thomas has wanted this job for three years.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he said either way he's selfish?
qa.a: Thomas felt torn and guilty, caught between his ambition and his lonely father.

qa.q: What helped Thomas and his family find a way forward?
qa.a: An honest talk with Papa and a shared plan, with Tarun helping with check-ups and Thomas calling nightly and visiting monthly.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about Thomas leaving?
qa.a: Papa seems worried about being alone but more worried about Thomas giving up his dream, so he supports him.

grounding: A young adult offered a job in another city weighs growth against a parent's needs, and honest talk and a shared plan reduce the sense of betrayal.

passage:
When the Mumbai offer came, I was twenty-two and I didn't tell my parents for two weeks. I'm Tanuja, the eldest daughter; in our house in Nagpur I handled Aai's medicines, Baba's bank work, my brother's forms.
My friend Parveen said, "You're allowed to go." But I kept thinking: if I leave, I'm betraying them. If I stay, I'm betraying myself.
Finally I sat with Aai and Baba. I told them the truth: I wanted the job, and I was scared of leaving them with everything.
Baba was quiet, then said, "We didn't raise you to hold the house forever." Aai cried a little, then made a list of what my brother could learn to do.
We made a plan. I taught my brother the bank work. A neighbour agreed to help Aai with the clinic visits. I went home every second weekend.
Looking back, it wasn't selfish to go. Hiding it was the only unfair part.

qa.q: How long did Tanuja wait before telling her parents about the offer?
qa.a: Tanuja didn't tell her parents for two weeks.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel about leaving?
qa.a: Tanuja felt torn, afraid of betraying her parents if she left and betraying herself if she stayed.

qa.q: What made the move work for the family?
qa.a: Honest talk and a shared plan, teaching her brother the bank work, a neighbour helping Aai, and regular visits home.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Tanuja's worry?
qa.a: Parveen sees that Tanuja is allowed to go and seems to want her friend to choose her own growth without guilt.

grounding: A young adult offered a job in another city weighs her growth against her parents' needs, and honest talk and shared plans reduce the sense of betrayal.

passage:
Placement mentor's note, final year, 18 March.
Jeevan, 21, came to me today after receiving the Hyderabad offer. He looked more worried than happy.
His father runs a hardware shop in Madurai and has assumed Jeevan will take over after college. Jeevan said, "If I go, I'm the son who left. If I stay, I'm giving up what I studied for." His friend Siddharth, who waited outside, told me later that Jeevan hadn't slept properly for a week.
I suggested that neither choice is selfish or noble on its own, and that the worst option is deciding without talking. We listed options: a two-year trial in Hyderabad; helping set up the shop's online orders from there; training his cousin, who is interested in the shop.
Next step: Jeevan will call his father this weekend and present these options, and ask what his father most needs. We'll meet again after.

qa.q: Where does Jeevan's father run a hardware shop?
qa.a: His father runs a hardware shop in Madurai.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he said "I'm the son who left"?
qa.a: Jeevan felt torn and guilty, worried about betraying his father and also about giving up his studies.

qa.q: Why is calling his father with options a wise next step?
qa.a: It turns the decision into an honest shared plan rather than a choice made alone, reducing the sense of betrayal on either side.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about his friend's week?
qa.a: Siddharth seems concerned for Jeevan, noticing he hadn't slept properly and waiting outside for him.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a young adult weighing a city job against his father's shop, and planning honest talk and shared options.

passage:
Payal's journal, Tuesday.
The Bengaluru offer came today. The actual job, the one with the lab. I squealed on the bus and a lady moved seats.
Then I got home and Mummy was massaging Papa's knee, and I didn't say anything for two hours.
Who takes him to physio if I go? Chhotu is in Class 9. Mummy's shop closes at eight.
Yusuf said on the phone, "You're not selfish for wanting it. You're not a saint for refusing it either." Annoying, but true.
At dinner I finally said it. Mummy went quiet. Papa said "Go" too fast.
So we sat with a notebook: physio twice a week, Chacha on Saturdays, a driver on Wednesdays, me home one weekend a month, a six-month trial, then we talk again.
Nobody's thrilled. Nobody feels betrayed either. I think that's the best tonight gets.

qa.q: How often will Payal come home, according to the plan?
qa.a: Payal will come home one weekend a month.

qa.q: Why didn't Payal mention the offer for two hours?
qa.a: Payal felt torn and guilty, seeing Mummy massaging Papa's knee and worrying about who would take him to physio.

qa.q: What made the family's notebook plan fair?
qa.a: It shared the care between Chacha, a driver and Payal's visits, and set a six-month trial with a promise to talk again.

qa.q: Why might Papa have said "Go" too fast?
qa.a: Papa probably didn't want to be a burden and felt proud of Payal, but the speed hints he was also hiding worry.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult weighing a job in another city against a parent's needs, and a family that talks honestly and plans together so neither choice feels like betrayal.
